text: I found the survey stakes on a Saturday morning, four orange flags hammered straight through my wife's tulip bed. Dennis Pruitt was standing on his porch with a coffee mug, watching me find them. "Contractor comes Tuesday," he called, cheerful as a radio host. "Six-foot cedar. You'll love it." I pulled one of the stakes out of the dirt and the bulb came up with it, roots dangling, split clean in half. My jaw locked so hard my molars ached. Twelve years of borrowing my ladder, my snowblower, my extension cord, and he couldn't knock on the door once before driving spikes into my yard. "You didn't think to ask me?" I said, and my voice came out low and flat, the way my father used to sound right before he broke something. Dennis shrugged and said the line was the line. I walked the stake over and laid it on his top step, very carefully, so I wouldn't throw it.

Mrs. Okonjo read the letter from the Hendersons three times at the kitchen table, and each time the paper crinkled a little more in her fist. They wanted a fence. Fine. But the attached sketch put it eighteen inches onto her side, swallowing the strip of lawn where her late husband had planted the fig tree in 1994. Her pulse thudded in her ears. She got up, sat down, got up again, and finally marched across in her house slippers without bothering to change. Ted Henderson opened the door smiling, which made it worse. "Your drawing is wrong," she said, jabbing a finger at the line. "That tree is mine. That ground is mine." He started explaining something about the county records, his tone slow and patient, as though she were a child who had misunderstood a cartoon. Her face went hot to the roots of her hair. "Do not speak to me like that," she said. "Get a real surveyor, or I get a lawyer. Choose by Friday."

The text came in while I was on a work call: "FYI fence going up tmrw, already got permit." That was it. No conversation, no question about the cost split he'd mentioned once in passing last spring, no question about whether I even wanted to stare at a wall of pressure-treated pine from my kitchen window for the rest of my life. I muted the call and typed a reply, deleted it, typed another, deleted that one too because it had words my mother would not approve of. My thumb was jabbing the screen hard enough to make it skip. Then a second text: "Invoice for your half attached." Eleven hundred dollars. I actually laughed, a short ugly bark that made my coworkers on the call ask if I was okay. I wasn't. I unmuted, said I had to go, and shut the laptop harder than it deserved. Then I put on my shoes and went next door, rehearsing every word through clenched teeth.

Rafael had been patient for three weeks of Brenda next door talking about her fence. He'd nodded at the brochures. He'd agreed that privacy was nice. What he had not agreed to was the crew that showed up at seven on a Sunday and started tearing out the hedge his grandmother had planted, the one that was very clearly on his side of the property marker. He came out barefoot, still in his undershirt, and grabbed the nearest worker's shoulder. "Stop. Stop right now. Who told you to cut that?" The man pointed at Brenda's window. Rafael's neck went tight, a cord of heat running from his collarbone up behind his ears. He pounded on her door with the side of his fist until the frame rattled. When she finally opened it in her robe, blinking, he could barely get the words out evenly. "That hedge was older than your house," he said. "You had no right. None."

The meeting at the homeowners' association was supposed to settle it. I brought printouts, the original plat map, a ruler. Lorraine Vasko brought her nephew, who apparently was a lawyer, or had watched enough of them on television. He talked for ten minutes about easements while she sat there nodding with her arms folded and a little smile I wanted to wipe off the folding table. When I finally got my turn, the chairman cut me off after thirty seconds to "keep things moving." Something in my chest went tight and hot, like a kettle right before the whistle. I stood up without meaning to. My chair scraped back across the linoleum loud enough that everyone flinched. "I have lived on that lot for twenty-two years," I said, and I could hear my own voice climbing. "Twenty-two years, and you're going to let her move the line because her nephew owns a tie?" Nobody answered. My hands were shaking as I gathered up my papers.

Kwame came home from a double shift to find the new chain-link fence already up, glinting under the streetlight, and his recycling bins locked on the wrong side of it. He stood in the driveway with his keys still in his hand, staring. The gate had a padlock. On the neighbor's side. He walked the length of it, slowly, his breath coming hard through his nose, and counted the posts. Seven of them sat squarely inside the line marked on his deed, which he knew by heart because he'd paid for the survey himself two years ago. He rattled the gate once, then again much harder, until the whole run of fence shuddered and sang. A light flicked on in the Albrechts' upstairs window. Good, he thought. Let them come down. Let them explain how a man works sixteen hours and comes home locked out of his own trash. He kept his finger pressed to their doorbell long after it had stopped being polite.

The envelope was taped to my door, not even mailed, and the landlord had used a smiley-face sticker to seal it. Inside: rent going up four hundred a month, effective in thirty days, "due to market conditions." I read it standing in the hallway with my grocery bags still cutting into my fingers. Four hundred. The same month the radiator had died for nine days in January and nobody came. The same year the ceiling in my bathroom had grown a brown water stain shaped like Florida, which I had photographed and emailed about six times. My face went hot and tight. I dropped the bags right there on the floor, a can of tomatoes rolling off toward the stairwell, and didn't even chase it. I called the management number and got voicemail, of course. "This is unit 4C," I said, and heard my voice shake with the effort of staying civil. "Call me back. Today."

Priya read the notice twice, then a third time out loud to her roommate, her voice rising with every sentence. The landlord was "reminding" them that guests could not stay more than two nights, citing a clause neither of them remembered. Her mother had flown in from Chennai for three weeks. The landlord knew this. He had helped carry the suitcase up. "He smiled at her," Priya said, slapping the letter down on the counter. "He actually smiled at my mother and asked about her flight." Her roommate tried to say something calming and Priya cut her off with a look. She paced to the window and back, arms crossed tight over her ribs, as if holding something in. Her jaw ached from clenching. When she finally sat down to write a reply, she pressed the pen into the paper so hard that it tore through on the second line, and she had to start again.

Dear Tenant, it began, which was the first insult, because Harold Brisbane had rented that apartment for nineteen years and the owner knew his name perfectly well. The letter said that his balcony plants constituted a "fire and structural hazard" and must be removed within seven days. Harold looked out at the tomatoes, the basil, the little lemon tree he'd nursed through four winters in a pot. His hands started trembling, not from age. He folded the letter into a tight square and then unfolded it and smoothed it flat on the table with the side of his palm, over and over, pressing harder each time. The new management company had bought the building in March. Since then: a parking fee, a laundry fee, a fee for the privilege of paying online. And now this. He picked up the phone, put it down, picked it up again. "Nineteen years," he said to the empty room, through his teeth.

I knew the landlord's letter was bad before I opened it because it came certified, and you only send something certified when you want proof the other person can't pretend they didn't get it. Notice of lease termination. No reason given, just a date, sixty days out, and a line thanking me for my tenancy. Thanking me. I'd fixed the garbage disposal myself. I'd repainted the bedroom on my own dime. I'd paid on the first of every month for six years while the upstairs guy paid whenever he felt like it. I could feel my heartbeat in my temples. I balled the letter up and threw it at the wall, and it bounced off and landed in the cat's water bowl, which somehow made it worse. Then I heard through the window the landlord's son telling someone on the phone that he was finally getting "his own place." I stood very still, breathing hard, until I could trust my legs to carry me downstairs.

Marisol had asked for the broken lock to be fixed in October. She'd asked again in November, and in December she'd started sleeping with a chair wedged under the handle. Now, in February, the landlord had finally written back: a letter informing her that she'd be charged a ninety-dollar "late processing fee" because her January check had arrived one day after the first. She stood at the mailboxes reading it while her son tugged at her sleeve. Her ears were ringing. One day. One day, for a check the post office had held. She crumpled the corner of the page in her fist without noticing. "Mami, what's wrong?" her son asked. "Nothing, mijo," she said, but her voice came out sharp, and he let go of her sleeve. She marched him up the stairs, unlocked the door that didn't lock, and sat down at the table to write a reply in capital letters, her pen gouging grooves into the paper.

The letter said we had forty-eight hours' notice for an "inspection," which in this building meant the owner's brother wandering through our bedroom taking photos with his phone. Last time he'd opened my dresser drawers. I'd found my underwear rearranged. I sat on the edge of the bed with the paper in my hand and felt my whole body go rigid, every muscle braced like I was about to be hit. My boyfriend said maybe it would be fine this time. I turned and looked at him, and he stopped talking. "It's not fine," I said. "It was never fine. He went through my things, Tomás." I got up and started pulling every drawer open and dumping the contents into a duffel bag, shoving clothes in so hard the zipper caught and wouldn't close. I yanked at it until the pull tab came off in my fingers. Then I sat down on the floor and called the tenants' union, and I did not let my voice soften once.

The board flipped from DELAYED to DELAYED again, a new time two hours later than the last new time, and Gideon felt something snap tight behind his eyes. His daughter's recital started at seven. He'd promised. He'd promised twice, actually, the second time after he missed her spring play. He walked up to the gate desk with his boarding pass crushed in one hand. The agent didn't look up from her screen. "Ma'am," he said. Nothing. "Ma'am." She lifted one finger, still typing. He set both palms flat on the counter and leaned in, his voice coming out loud enough that the people in line behind him went quiet. "I have been standing here for four hours with no information. Four. Hours. Is there a plane or is there not a plane?" She finally looked at him, flat-eyed, and told him to step back. He didn't, not right away. His pulse was going so hard he could feel it in his neck.

They had already boarded us. That's what got me. We'd been sitting on the plane for ninety minutes, seatbelts on, air system off, a toddler kicking the back of my seat in a steady metronome, when the captain came on and said with a little chuckle that there was "a minor paperwork issue." A chuckle. I unbuckled and stood up, which you're not supposed to do, and the flight attendant told me to sit down, and I said I'd sit down when someone told me what was happening. My shirt was sticking to my back. Every breath of that stale air made it worse. The man next to me muttered "here we go" like I was the problem, and I turned and stared at him until he looked away. I sat, eventually, but I kept my fists balled on my knees, knuckles white, grinding my teeth, counting the rivets on the overhead bin to keep from screaming.

Yuki had been rebooked three times. The fourth time the app pinged her, she was standing at a food court counter holding a twelve-dollar sandwich, and she read the notification and simply set the sandwich down and walked away from it. Cancelled. The next available seat was Thursday. It was Monday. She stalked toward the customer service desk, weaving around people with their rolling bags, cutting a little too close, not caring when she clipped someone's suitcase. The line was forty people deep. Ahead of her, a man in a business suit was being booked onto a flight that left in an hour. She heard the agent say "since you're Platinum" and felt her face burn. "Excuse me," she said, loudly, to no one in particular, "so the rest of us just live here now?" A few people laughed nervously. She wasn't joking. Her hands were trembling as she pulled up the airline's complaint form and began to type.

"Weather," the agent said, and I looked past her shoulder at the window behind the gate, where the sky was a brilliant, cloudless blue and the sun was bouncing off the wing of our plane. "Weather where?" I asked. She said at the destination. I pulled out my phone and showed her the forecast for Denver: sunny, sixty-two. She shrugged and said that's what the system told her. I felt the heat climb up my neck into my face, and my voice came out tight and very quiet, which people who know me understand is worse than loud. "You canceled it because it's half empty. Just say that." She said she couldn't comment. Behind me someone muttered agreement. I'd missed my brother's engagement dinner for this, and I'd been lied to in a voice of perfect courtesy. I took my boarding pass back from her, tore it in half, then in half again, and dropped the pieces on her counter.

Abdullah had spent the night on the airport floor, his jacket rolled under his head, because the airline had run out of hotel vouchers by the time they got to his row. At six a.m., stiff and unshaven, he went to the gate and was told his rebooked flight had been delayed. Again. The muscles across his shoulders bunched. He did not shout. He'd seen a man get escorted out the night before for shouting. Instead he leaned close and spoke slowly, every word clipped and hard. "I want to speak to your supervisor. I want your name. And I want it written down that I was promised a hotel and I slept beside a trash can." The young agent swallowed. Abdullah watched him, unblinking, and felt no pity at all, only a hot, steady pressure behind his ribs that had been building for fourteen hours and had nowhere left to go but out through his voice.

The gate changed for the third time, from B12 to B40 to C7, and Martina hauled her carry-on and her sleeping five-year-old across the airport for the third time, the little girl's dead weight dragging at her arm. At C7 the screen said the flight was delayed indefinitely. Indefinitely. She laid her daughter down across two chairs and stood there with her hands on her hips, breathing hard, sweat prickling under her collar. A gate agent was chatting and laughing with a pilot nearby, both holding coffees. Martina walked over. "Sorry to interrupt your break," she said, not sorry at all, her voice dripping with it. "Do either of you know when we're leaving, or is that classified?" The pilot's smile vanished. The agent opened her mouth to answer and Martina cut her off. "Don't tell me to check the app. The app has lied to me all day." Her hands were shaking. She shoved them in her pockets.

The results had been sitting in my patient portal for six days before anyone called me. Six days. I found them myself, at eleven at night, scrolling through numbers I didn't understand with a red flag next to one of them. I spent the whole night searching medical terms, sick and wide awake. When the nurse finally phoned the next afternoon, she said, breezy as anything, "Oh, the doctor just hasn't had a chance to review them." My grip on the phone tightened until the case creaked. "There's a red flag on my thyroid panel," I said, "and nobody had a chance?" She said she understood my frustration. She did not. I said I wanted an appointment that week, not in a month, and when she said the earliest was five weeks out I heard myself say, "Then find me a different doctor," in a voice I barely recognized, hard and cold and loud enough that my cat fled the room.

Doctor Anand finally came into the exam room forty minutes late, glanced at a tablet, and told Nadia her test was "probably nothing" before she had even sat back down. Then he said they'd just repeat it in three months. Nadia stared at him. Three months ago another doctor in this same building had said the same words about the same lump. She felt her face go tight, heat flooding up from her collarbone. "Did you read my chart?" she asked. He looked faintly surprised. "This is the second time," she said, her voice getting louder despite herself. "The second time someone in this office has told me to wait. I want a biopsy. I want it scheduled before I leave this room." He began to explain about guidelines, and she gripped the edges of the paper-covered table so hard it tore under her fingers. "I'm not leaving," she said. "Go read it. I'll wait."

They had sent Walter's blood work to the wrong lab. That was the explanation, delivered over the phone by a receptionist who sounded like she was eating lunch: the sample was gone, he'd need to come back in, fast for twelve hours again, take another half day off work. He'd already done this once. He'd already sat in that plastic chair with the tourniquet biting his arm and watched the tech miss the vein twice. "So it's my problem," he said. She said no one was saying that. "You just did," he snapped. His free hand found the edge of the kitchen counter and gripped it. Through the window he could see his truck, the one he'd driven forty minutes each way for the first draw. His neck was hot. He listened to her offer an appointment next Wednesday, and he said nothing for so long that she asked if he was still there. "Yes," he said through his teeth. "Unfortunately."

I got my test results in a letter addressed to my sister. Same last name, same clinic, and some clerk had put my diagnosis in her envelope and hers in mine, so the way I learned I had diabetes was my sister calling me, crying, at work, to ask why I hadn't told her. I hadn't told her because I didn't know. I stood in the break room with the phone pressed to my ear and felt my whole body go hot, like a fever coming on all at once. I drove straight to the clinic, parked crooked across two spaces, and walked to the front desk holding both letters out like evidence. "Who mailed these?" I said. The receptionist started to say something about privacy policy. "Privacy?" I said, and my voice cracked straight up into a shout. "My sister read my blood sugar before I did!" The whole waiting room turned to look. I didn't care.

Ingrid's father kept insisting he was fine, that the doctor had said the scan looked "much better," and Ingrid kept nodding while she read the printout over his shoulder and saw the word "progression" in bold. He had lied. Or the doctor had lied to him, which was worse. She took the paper from his hands, gently, and then walked into the hallway and found the oncologist at the nurses' station. Her heart was slamming. "You told my father his scan looked better." The doctor began to say she'd wanted to keep his spirits up. Ingrid felt her vision narrow. "He is eighty-one years old," she said, each word distinct and hard as a stone set down on the counter. "He gets to know what's happening in his own body. You do not get to decide that for him." Her voice didn't rise, but the nurse beside them stopped typing. Ingrid didn't move until the doctor agreed to come back into the room.

The text said "Your results are ready! Log in to view," and when Darnell logged in he found out his insurance had denied the follow-up scan the results said he needed. Right there on the same screen. Abnormal finding, next steps recommended, claim not approved. He read it three times. Then he picked up the phone and called the insurance company and sat on hold for fifty-two minutes listening to the same eight bars of synthesized jazz, his knee bouncing harder and harder under the table until the coffee in his mug sloshed over the rim. When a person finally picked up and told him the scan was "not medically necessary," he stood up so fast the chair tipped over behind him. "Your own doctor's note says it's necessary," he said. "Are you a doctor?" She wasn't. He made her read the note aloud, line by line, and he did not say thank you when she finished.

Ms. Delacroix dropped the exam on my desk face down, and when I flipped it over there was a sixty-one circled in red, and next to my essay answer, the one I'd spent the most time on, she'd written "Did you copy this?" I hadn't. I'd stayed up until two writing practice versions of it. My ears started burning, and I could feel my face going red, which made it worse because everyone could see. Jordan behind me leaned over to look and I covered the page with my forearm so hard my elbow banged the desk. When the bell rang, I didn't leave. I walked up to her desk and put the paper down in front of her. "I didn't copy it," I said, and my voice was shaking, not because I was scared. "You can ask me anything about it right now. Go ahead." She looked at me for a long time. I didn't blink once.

Luca got his midterm back with a C and a note that said "missing work shown," on the calculus problem where he'd filled the entire back of the page with work. The professor had simply not turned the page over. He could see it from here: the back, crowded with his cramped handwriting, every step, every integral, not a single red mark on it. His jaw clenched. He flipped the paper back and forth twice, his breath hissing out through his nose. Around him people were comparing grades, laughing, groaning. He wasn't listening. He was already standing, already walking down the lecture hall steps two at a time, the paper gripped so tight it creased. The professor was packing his bag. "You didn't read the back," Luca said, louder than he meant to, and several heads turned. He slapped the exam onto the lectern, back side up. "Twenty points. You took twenty points off for work that's right there."

Our teacher handed back the tests in order of score, highest first, out loud, and she did it every time, and every time I sat there while my name didn't come and didn't come. When she finally got to me she said, "Fatima, let's talk after class," in that sorrowful voice, so the whole room heard. I could feel everybody's eyes. My chest went tight and my hands went cold and then hot. I'd gotten a seventy-two. That's not even failing. I took the paper and folded it in half, then in quarters, then into the smallest square I could manage, pressing each crease flat with my thumbnail until it hurt. After class she started telling me she was "worried," and I cut her off. "Then don't read the scores out," I said. She looked shocked that I'd said anything at all. "Everybody knows I'm last now. Thanks for that." I walked out before she could answer, and I let the door bang.

Henrik had told the teacher, weeks ago, that his son had dyslexia and was entitled to extra time. It was in the file. It was in two emails. And still Aksel came home with the history exam half blank and a big red forty-five, and when Henrik asked what happened the boy said quietly that Mr. Fenwick had collected the papers when the bell rang, same as everyone. Henrik sat very still at the kitchen table. Then he got up and stood at the sink and ran the cold water over his wrists, which his own father used to do, and it didn't help. His heart was pounding. He dried his hands, opened the laptop, and began to type, deleting each sentence as it came out because each one was too vicious to send. Aksel watched him from the doorway. "Are you upset with me?" Henrik stopped, turned, and pulled him into a hug. "No," he said. "Not with you. Never with you."

I recognized my own answer on the exam the professor projected as the "model response" for the class. My exact sentences. Only, the name at the top wasn't mine; it was Brett's, the guy who'd borrowed my notes the night before. And my own paper, when it came back to me, had a fifty-eight and the comment "seems derivative." I sat there with blood roaring in my ears, staring at the projection while the professor praised Brett's "original thinking." Brett didn't look at me. He was staring very hard at his laptop. My knee was bouncing so violently the whole row of connected seats shook, and the girl next to me shifted away. I wanted to stand up and say it right there, in front of all two hundred people. Instead I wrote down the time, the slide number, the exact phrases, my pen digging into the notebook, and after class I followed Brett out into the hallway and said his name, hard, just once.

Sofia's exam came back with a B-minus, which she could have lived with, except that every single point deducted was for her spelling, on a biology test, from a teacher who had told the class in September that spelling wouldn't count. She went down the page with her finger: minus two for "mitocondria," minus two for "chlorofil," minus one for a missing comma. The heat climbed up her throat. She raised her hand. When Mr. Abernathy came over, she asked, very politely, whether he remembered saying spelling didn't count. He said he'd changed his mind. "When?" she asked. "When did you tell us?" He said he didn't need to announce every policy. Sofia's hand closed around her pencil until the edges dug into her palm. "Yes, you do," she said, and the room went quiet. "You have to tell us the rules before you grade us on them. That's what rules are." Her voice wobbled, but she did not look down.

I saw Corinne before she saw me, standing in the cereal aisle with her cart, and my hands tightened on the handle of my own cart until the plastic creaked. Eight years. Eight years since she'd taken the business we'd built together, the bakery with both our names on the sign, and quietly signed it over to her husband's cousin while I was in the hospital having my gallbladder out. She turned. Her face lit up like we were long-lost sisters. "Oh my God, Wren!" She actually opened her arms. I didn't move. I could feel my heartbeat in my throat, hot and thick. "Don't," I said. She laughed, uncertain, and started saying how she'd always meant to call. I looked at the box of granola in her cart, the expensive kind, and thought about the loan I was still paying off. "You had eight years of phones," I said, and I steered around her so close our carts clanged.

Marcus recognized the laugh first, booming from two aisles over, and every muscle in his back went stiff. Desmond. His best friend from college, the best man at his wedding, the guy who'd borrowed six thousand dollars for a "sure thing" and then stopped answering texts. And here he was by the deli counter, tanned, in a new jacket, joking with the woman slicing turkey. Marcus pushed his cart straight up to him without deciding to. "Des." Desmond turned, and for a second his face went blank with panic before he forced a grin. "Marcus! Man, it's been forever." "Four years," Marcus said. His voice was flat and his ears were ringing. "Four years, three months. I kept track. Funny how that works when someone owes you money." The deli woman stopped slicing. Desmond's grin wobbled. He started talking about a rough patch, and Marcus just stood there, jaw clenched, letting him dig, refusing to help him out of the hole.

Hyun-woo almost didn't recognize her, but then she said his name in that bright, careless voice, and it all came back at once: the high school reunion she'd organized and "forgotten" to invite him to, the group chat he'd later found where she'd made a running joke out of his stutter. Jessamyn. She was holding a melon and smiling. "We should get coffee!" she said. He felt the old heat climbing up his neck, the same flush he used to get in the cafeteria, except now it wasn't shame. It was something harder, something that made his fingers curl into his palms. "No," he said. Just that. It came out without a single catch, smooth as glass, and he was almost surprised. She blinked. "Oh, come on, don't be like that, we were kids." He set his basket down on the floor between them. "You were seventeen and you knew exactly what you were doing," he said, and he walked out without his groceries.

I'd been telling myself for months I was over it, so I wasn't ready for how hard my pulse jumped when I came around the end of the produce section and there was Lupe, weighing tomatoes. My oldest friend. The one who'd told my ex everything I'd confided in her the week we broke up, every word, so that he could use it against me in mediation. She looked up and her mouth fell open. "Ana. Hi." I didn't say hi. I could feel my lips pressing together so hard they went numb. She started in on how she'd been meaning to reach out, how things had been complicated, and the more she talked the hotter my face got, until my eyes stung. "Complicated," I repeated. A tomato rolled off the scale and splatted on the floor, and neither of us looked at it. "He quoted you, Lupe. In front of a lawyer. Word for word." My voice cracked, and I hated that, and I turned and walked away fast before it cracked again.

Old Mr. Kowalczyk was reaching for a can of peaches on the top shelf when he heard the voice behind him, and his hand stopped mid-air. Stanley Brandt. Forty years they'd played cards together every Thursday, until the night Stanley stood up at the town council meeting and voted to sell the park where Kowalczyk's late wife used to walk the dog. Now Stanley was beaming at him as though nothing had happened. "Jerzy! How's the hip?" Kowalczyk lowered his arm slowly. His jaw worked, the muscles bunching under his loose cheeks. "Ask the bulldozers how my hip is," he said, and his voice came out loud, louder than he'd used in years, startling a young mother at the end of the aisle. Stanley's smile faltered. "Now, Jerzy, that was business." Kowalczyk took the can down after all, held it a moment, weighing it in his trembling hand, and then put it in his own basket, very deliberately, and turned his back.

The checkout line was the worst place for it, trapped between the magazine rack and a man with a cart full of soda, when Delphine felt a tap on her shoulder and turned to find Odile, who had once been her closest friend and who had, three years ago, slept with Delphine's husband. Odile's eyes were wet. "I've thought about you every day," she said. Delphine's whole body went rigid. Her hands, holding a carton of eggs, began to squeeze, and she had to set the carton on the belt before she crushed it. "Have you," she said. Her voice was low and shaking. People were staring. Good. "Every day, you thought about me. That's lovely. I thought about you too, Odile. At the lawyer's office. While I packed his shirts." The cashier had stopped scanning. Odile opened her mouth, and Delphine raised one hand, palm out, an inch from her face. "Not here. Not ever," she said, and she pushed her eggs forward.

The engine light came on at the third traffic light and the car died at the fourth, right in the middle of the intersection, with a bus honking behind me. I turned the key. Nothing. I turned it again, harder, as if that would help, and then I slammed my palm against the steering wheel so hard the horn went off and the bus driver honked back, long and vicious. I'd just paid twelve hundred dollars to get this exact problem fixed. Twelve hundred dollars and a week of taking two buses. My face was burning. I had a presentation at nine that I'd rehearsed until midnight. I called the mechanic, and when the receptionist cheerfully told me that the warranty didn't cover "related issues," I heard myself say, "It's the same issue, it's literally the same part," in a voice that rose so high it cracked. A guy in a pickup leaned out and yelled at me to move. I yelled back.

Thabo had told his brother-in-law not to borrow the car. He'd said it twice, clearly. And now, on the shoulder of the highway at seven forty in the morning, with the hood up and steam pouring out of the radiator, he found the empty coolant jug wedged under the passenger seat, along with a note in Sipho's handwriting: "Topped it up, you're welcome." Thabo crushed the note in his fist. The heat from the engine and the heat in his chest were starting to feel like the same thing. He dialed Sipho, who answered sleepily. "You put water in it," Thabo said. "Just water. In January." Sipho started to protest, and Thabo cut across him, his voice going hoarse. "The block is cracked. Do you know what a cracked block costs? Do you have any idea?" A truck roared past, rocking the car. He kicked the front tire, once, hard enough to hurt his toes through his work boot, and didn't even flinch.

It was the third time in a month. Isabela was standing on the side of the ring road in her nurse's scrubs, in the drizzle, watching her ancient hatchback tick and cool, and she realized she was grinding her teeth so hard her temples throbbed. Her shift started in twenty minutes. Nobody at the hospital would care that her alternator had died; they'd care that the night nurse had to stay late again, and the night nurse would give her that look. She called a tow. Ninety minutes, they said. She called her husband. He didn't pick up, because of course he didn't, because he was asleep in the bed she'd gotten up early to leave. She typed a message to him, all capitals, and hit send before she could think. Then she opened the driver's door and slammed it shut, and opened it and slammed it again, until a woman jogging past gave her a wide berth and Isabela glared at her too.

The tow truck driver looked at my car, looked at me, and said, "Sweetheart, did you check the gas?" I had checked the gas. I had a full tank. I had a dashboard full of warning lights and smoke coming out of the wheel well, and he wanted to know if I'd checked the gas. I could feel my jaw tightening into a shape that made my teeth ache. "The transmission is gone," I said, very evenly. "I know it's the transmission because I've driven stick since I was fourteen and I heard it go." He chuckled and said okay, okay, and started explaining how transmissions work, slowly, like a nursery rhyme. I stood there in my office clothes with my hands balled up in my coat pockets, nails digging into my palms, while he talked. When he finally said, "Let's just take a look," and popped the hood, I said, "It's not under the hood," and I didn't bother to soften it at all.

Mehmet's boss had already written him up twice for being late, and on the morning his van coughed and died on the bridge, he sat behind the wheel for one long second with his eyes shut and his hands clamped on the wheel, knuckles pale, breathing in and out through his nose like a bull. Then he got out into the wind. Cars streamed around him, honking, one driver flipping him off as if he'd stalled on purpose. He flipped him off right back, both hands, shouting something in Turkish his mother would have slapped him for. He called the boss. Voicemail. He called again and left a message that started polite and ended with him saying, "And if you write me up for this, you can drive the van yourself." He hung up, shaking, and only then did he notice he'd been kicking the guardrail the entire time and his shin was throbbing.

I knew exactly who to blame. The quick-lube place on Fifth had changed my oil the day before, and that morning, ten minutes into my commute, the oil pressure light came on and the engine started knocking like someone was trapped inside with a hammer. I pulled over and checked the dipstick with shaking fingers. Bone dry. They'd drained it and never refilled it. I stood beside the car with the dipstick in my hand and felt the blood pounding in my face. That engine had two hundred thousand miles on it and I'd babied every one of them. I had the receipt in my glove box. I called the shop and the kid who answered said the manager wasn't in yet. "Then you write this down," I said, and I spelled my name, slowly, every letter, and then I told him precisely what his shop had done to my car, in a voice so quiet and so cold that he stopped saying "sir."

Curfew was eleven. At eleven-forty Graciela was sitting on the stairs in her bathrobe with the phone in her lap, and at twelve-fifteen she was pacing the hallway, and by one she had called her son's cell nine times and listened to it go straight to voicemail nine times. His location was turned off. He'd turned it off. She stopped in front of the door and pressed her forehead to the cool wood, breathing hard. The worry had burned down into something sharper. When the headlights finally swung across the window at one thirty-seven and Mateo slipped in, shoes in hand, trying to be quiet, she was standing right there. He jumped. "Mom—" "Don't," she said. Her voice came out low and shaking. "Don't you say a single word to me until you've looked at your phone." He looked. Nine missed calls. "You switched off your location," she said, her teeth clenched. "On purpose. So I wouldn't know."

I'd told her that the party at the Fischers' house was off limits, and she'd said fine, she was going to Kendra's to study, and at midnight Kendra's mother called me to ask if my daughter was all right because Kendra had snuck out too. I sat at the kitchen table with my car keys in front of me and every light in the house switched on, and I could feel my pulse ticking in my jaw. Lied to my face. Looked me right in the eyes and lied. I picked up the keys and put them down and picked them up again. I wasn't going to go drag her out of a party in front of her friends. I wasn't. I was going to sit here. When the door finally opened at two, I didn't get up. "Study go well?" I said. Pippa froze in the doorway. I could hear how hard and flat my voice was, and I watched her hear it too.

Ezekiel heard the car before he saw it: tires squealing around the corner of their quiet street, music thumping so loud the windows hummed, and then a door, and laughter, and the car peeling off again. He was on the porch before his son reached the steps. The boy smelled of beer. Ezekiel's chest went tight, his hands went hot, and the four hours he'd spent picturing ditches and hospital beds curdled all at once into something that made his voice boom. "Who was driving that car?" Jonah mumbled a name. "Was he drinking?" Jonah shrugged, and that shrug did it. Ezekiel grabbed the porch railing so hard a splinter bit into his palm. "You got in a car," he said, each word heavier than the last, "with a drunk boy, at two in the morning, and you're shrugging at me." Jonah finally looked up and saw his father's face and stopped shrugging.

The text arrived at twelve fifty-two: "staying at sams, sorry forgot to say." Sorry forgot to say. Rosalind read it standing in the dark kitchen where she had been standing, more or less, since eleven, watching the street, making deals with God. She'd called the hospital at twelve-thirty. She'd called the police non-emergency line at twelve forty-five, and a tired officer had been kind to her, and she'd felt like an idiot. Now her hand trembled around the phone. She typed "Come home now" and then deleted it, and typed it again, and this time added "or I am driving over there." Her thumb hit send so hard the phone slipped. She stalked to the hall closet and yanked down her coat, the hanger clattering to the floor, and stood with one arm in the sleeve, breathing hard, staring at the door. Forgot. As if her daughter could forget that her mother was lying awake.

My son came home at three a.m. with a dent in my car. Not a scratch. A dent, the size of a dinner plate, in the passenger door. I'd been up since midnight, rehearsing whatever I was going to say, and in all the versions I'd rehearsed I'd been calm. Then he walked in and said, "Before you freak out," and I felt every rehearsed sentence evaporate in the heat rising up my throat. "Before I what?" I said. My voice went up and up. "Before I what, Dev?" He said it was a pole in a parking lot, not his fault, a friend was guiding him. I said I didn't care whose fault the pole was. I said he was supposed to be home by twelve. I said a lot of things, too fast, and I slammed my palm down on the counter so hard the fruit bowl jumped. He flinched, and I hated that, and I didn't stop.

At one a.m. Magnus finally heard the key scrape in the lock, and he didn't get up from the armchair in the dark living room. He just reached over and switched on the lamp. His daughter Liv yelped. "God, Dad, you scared me." He didn't answer right away. His fingers were drumming on the armrest, a hard, fast rhythm he couldn't seem to stop. "Do you know what I was doing at eleven," he said finally, "when you were supposed to walk through that door?" She muttered something about her phone dying. "At eleven I was calling your friends. At midnight I was calling their parents. At twelve-thirty I was in the car, driving around the lake, looking at the water." His voice cracked on that last word, and he stood up abruptly, and she took a step back. "Your phone died," he repeated, flat and hard. "And everyone else's phone died too? All of them, at once?" She said nothing. He stared at her.

My manager closed the door behind me, which she never does, and said, "So, about the Hollis account." I already knew. I'd landed the Hollis account. I'd flown to Cleveland twice on my own weekends to land it. And at the all-hands that morning, the VP had thanked Garrett for it, by name, while Garrett sat there nodding modestly. Now she wanted to "align on the narrative." I felt the blood rise into my face and stay there. "The narrative," I said. She said Garrett was "client-facing" now and it made sense for continuity. My fingers found the arms of the chair and gripped them. "I wrote every slide in that deck. His name isn't on one of them." She sighed, like I was being difficult. That sigh. I leaned forward. "Don't sigh at me," I said, very quietly. "Tell me why you let him take it." She didn't have an answer, and I sat there, breathing hard, waiting, not letting her look away.

Vikram was called into Mr. Hale's office at four fifty-five on a Friday, which everyone knew meant something bad, and Hale didn't even ask him to sit. "We're going to need you to come in Saturday and Sunday. The Delgado project slipped." Vikram stood very still. The Delgado project had slipped because Hale had changed the specifications three times in two weeks and ignored every email Vikram sent warning him. Vikram's daughter had a birthday party on Saturday. He'd told Hale a month ago. "It slipped," Vikram said, "because you changed the scope on Tuesday." Hale's eyebrows went up. "Excuse me?" Vikram's heart was hammering now, his hands cold, his neck hot. He'd swallowed it for three years. "You heard me. I have the emails. I will not be here Saturday." Hale started to say something about attitude, and Vikram turned and walked out, leaving the door open behind him, his whole body humming like a struck wire.

The manager's office smelled like his cologne and burnt coffee, and I sat in the low chair he kept for visitors, the one that made you look up at him, while he explained that my request for a raise had been "declined at this time." Then he told me, in the same breath, that they'd be adding the Northside territory to my responsibilities. More work, same pay. And then, as if it were a kindness, he said he'd put me up for Employee of the Month. My fingernails were digging half-moons into my palms. I could feel a vein jumping in my temple. "I've trained the last four people you hired," I said. "Two of them make more than I do." He blinked and asked how I knew that. "Because they told me," I said, louder, "because they were embarrassed for me." He started to say salaries were confidential, and I stood up out of that ridiculous little chair so I could look him in the eye.

Beatrix was ushered into the office to find not only her manager but someone from HR, a woman with a folder and a sympathetic head tilt. A complaint had been filed, they said. About her "tone" in meetings. Beatrix felt her spine straighten, her chin lift. She asked who filed it. They couldn't say. She asked what she had said. They read a line from the folder: she had told a colleague his numbers were wrong. "Were they wrong?" she asked. The manager shifted. "That's not really the point." "It's exactly the point," Beatrix said, and she heard her voice snap like a flag in wind. "His numbers were wrong by two hundred thousand dollars, and I said so, politely, in front of the people who would have signed off on them. And now I'm in here." The HR woman tilted her head even further. Beatrix's hands were flat on the table, pressed so hard her fingertips went white.

"Close the door, Ferris." I closed the door. My manager, Lyle, had a printout in front of him: my timesheets, highlighted in yellow. He wanted to talk about my "pattern of late arrivals." Every highlighted morning was a day I'd come in at nine-fifteen instead of nine because I was dropping my mother at dialysis, which Lyle had approved, in writing, in March. I told him so. He said he didn't recall that conversation. My ears started ringing. I pulled up the email on my phone, the one with his name at the bottom and the words "of course, take whatever time you need," and I slid it across the desk to him, and my hand was trembling so badly the phone skidded and nearly went off the edge. He read it. He said, "Well, that was before the reorganization." I just stared at him, feeling the heat crawl up my neck, and said, "My mother's kidneys didn't get reorganized, Lyle."

Chen Jing sat across from her supervisor while he praised her work for fifteen minutes and then, almost as an afterthought, mentioned that the promotion was going to Kyle. Kyle, who had been there eleven months. Kyle, whom she had trained. "He's got real leadership presence," the supervisor said, spreading his hands. Chen Jing smiled, because she always smiled, and felt her molars grind behind the smile until her jaw throbbed. She asked what leadership presence meant, specifically. He said it was hard to define. "Try," she said, and the smile was gone now, and her voice had dropped into a register she had never used in this building. He stammered something about confidence in meetings, about speaking up. She leaned forward. "I am speaking up," she said. "Right now. Is this the presence you mean?" He laughed nervously. She didn't laugh. She sat very straight and let the silence stretch until he was the one who had to look away.

I was clearing out the attic before the house sale when I found the shoebox, and inside, under some old Christmas cards, a letter in my father's handwriting addressed to my mother, dated the year I was born. I read it sitting on a dusty trunk with the bare bulb swinging over my head. He'd known. He'd known about the other family the whole time, the one in Tucson, and he'd written to my mother asking her to "keep the peace for the children's sake." She had. For thirty-one years. My hands were shaking so badly the paper rattled. I thought about every Thanksgiving, every speech he'd made at the dinner table about honesty, about how a man's word was all he had. I felt the heat rising in my throat, behind my eyes, choking me. I stood up too fast and cracked my head on a rafter and didn't even rub it. I just folded the letter and put it in my pocket and went downstairs to call my brother.

The letter had been tucked inside an old atlas, and Annika almost threw it away before she saw her own name on the envelope, in her grandmother's spidery script. It was from a scholarship board in Stockholm. Dated 1987. Offering her, at eighteen, a full place at the conservatory. She'd never seen it. She'd been told she wasn't selected. She'd taken a job at the post office instead and stopped playing the piano altogether by twenty-five. Annika sat back on her heels in the dust, the letter trembling in her fingers, and felt something tighten in her chest until breathing hurt. Her mother had opened it. Her mother had read it and hidden it and let her cry for a week. Annika pressed her lips together so hard they went numb. Downstairs, she could hear her mother humming in the kitchen, perfectly content, and the sound of it made Annika's hands curl into fists around the paper.

Under a pile of moth-eaten coats in the attic, Bashir found a bundle of letters tied with string. One was from his uncle Farid to his father, dated the spring the family restaurant was sold. "I'll handle the paperwork," his uncle had written. "Your share will come after closing." Bashir knew how that story ended. His father had died waiting for that share, still believing his brother would make it right. And here was Farid's handwriting, so smug, so sure of himself, admitting in a postscript that the buyer had paid "a little more than we told the others." Bashir read the line again and felt his face flush hot. His teeth clenched until his jaw clicked. He thought of Farid at the funeral, weeping loudest, clutching Bashir's mother's hands. He climbed down the ladder so fast he missed a rung and banged his knee, and he didn't even stop to feel it. He was already dialing.

It was a letter I had written myself, at sixteen, to my best friend Caroline, and it had never been sent. I'd forgotten it existed. I unfolded it in the attic of my parents' house, smiling, expecting something silly, and instead read my own teenage handwriting describing what my stepfather said to me when my mother wasn't home. I'd put it in an envelope and never mailed it, because my mother had found it first. I remembered now. I remembered her reading it and telling me I was being dramatic, and tucking it away somewhere, and that was the end of it. My hands went cold and then burning hot. I sat on the attic floor with my knees pulled up and the letter crushed against my chest and felt my whole body shake with something that wasn't sadness, something that wanted to climb down the ladder and walk into the kitchen and put this letter on the table in front of her and make her read it again.

The letter was from the insurance company, dated 2009, and Lorenzo found it wedged behind a broken drawer in the attic his brother had refused to clear out for years. It confirmed payment of the policy on their mother's house after the fire. Ninety-two thousand dollars. Paid to the executor. Lorenzo's brother had been the executor, and Lorenzo had been told, at the time, with a sad shake of the head, that the policy had lapsed. He'd believed it. He'd lent his brother money that same year. He stood under the low beams with the paper in one hand and felt his blood pound in his ears. The attic was hot and close, and the heat seemed to gather in his face. He put the letter in his shirt pocket and buttoned the pocket shut, slowly, deliberately, one button, and then he went down the stairs one at a time, each step landing harder than the last.

Grace was hunting for her old yearbooks when she found the stack of letters held together with a rubber band that crumbled at her touch. They were addressed to her, from her biological father, and they spanned eleven years. Birthday cards. Letters asking if she'd like to visit. A photograph of a man holding a toddler she slowly realized was her. Every single envelope had been opened. Her adoptive mother had told her, over and over, that he never wanted to know her. Grace's chest felt like it had been packed with hot sand. She tore through the stack, reading faster, her breath coming short and ragged, her vision blurring at the edges. The last letter, dated when she was fifteen, said he wouldn't write again if she didn't want him to. She hadn't known to want anything. She slammed the lid of the trunk so hard that dust rose in a cloud around her, and she sat in it, coughing, shaking, fists clenched.

Twenty minutes before the guests were due, I opened the fridge for the lamb and found an empty platter with a smear of marinade on it and a sticky note in my roommate's handwriting: "Sorry!! Got hungry, will replace." I stood there with the fridge door open and the cold air pouring over my feet and felt every muscle in my shoulders lock up. Will replace. With what? The butcher closed at six. It was six-forty. I'd marinated that lamb for two days. I slammed the fridge so hard the magnets fell off and scattered across the floor. Then I stood at the counter with my palms flat on the cutting board, breathing through my nose, while the potatoes boiled over behind me and hissed on the burner. I didn't even turn the heat down. I texted Noor: "You ate the dinner. For eight people." My thumbs were jabbing the screen. Then the doorbell rang, early, and I had to smile.

Aurelio had asked his husband for exactly one thing: pick up the fish on the way home. Not a complicated thing. Branzino, two of them, already ordered, already paid for, waiting at the counter with Aurelio's name on them. And at seven-fifteen, with the risotto at the stage where you cannot stop stirring and the doorbell due to ring at seven-thirty, Clément walked in swinging an empty grocery bag and said, "Wait, was that today?" Aurelio's wooden spoon stopped moving. The risotto began, very faintly, to catch on the bottom of the pan. He felt heat rush into his face that had nothing to do with the stove. "I wrote it on the board," he said, pointing the spoon at the fridge, where FISH was written in letters three inches high. "I texted you at four. I texted you at six." Clément laughed nervously. Aurelio didn't. He turned back to the pan and stirred so hard rice flew over the rim.

The oven died at six fifty-two. Just clicked off, mid-roast, the light inside going dark, the fan winding down to silence, while Precious stood there in her apron with her mother-in-law due at seven-thirty. The same mother-in-law who had said, at the wedding, that she hoped Precious would "learn to cook properly." Precious jabbed at the buttons. Nothing. She flipped the breaker. Nothing. She smacked the side of the oven with her open palm, hard enough to sting, and then again, and her eyes were burning now and her breath was coming in short, hot bursts. The landlord had promised to replace this oven in August. She called him and got his voicemail greeting, the one where he laughed. She hung up mid-laugh and threw the phone onto the couch across the room, where it bounced off a cushion and hit the floor. The chicken sat there, half-cooked and pale, mocking her.

My sister had promised to come early and help, and at seven, with guests arriving at seven-thirty, she texted that she was "running a little behind" with a winking face. I set my knife down very carefully on the board, because if I hadn't set it down carefully I would have flung it into the sink. I had six dishes in progress and two hands. The sauce needed whisking, the bread needed to go in, the salad wasn't even washed. She'd volunteered. She'd insisted, actually, said it was the least she could do since it was her birthday dinner I was cooking. Her birthday. I felt my face get hot and tight, a pressure behind my eyes, and I grabbed the whisk and attacked the sauce until it splattered across the backsplash and onto my shirt. I didn't wipe it off. When she finally arrived at seven-forty, carrying flowers and apologies, I handed her the salad spinner without looking at her and said, "Wash."

Takeshi had spent all afternoon on the dashi, skimming and straining, tasting and adjusting, and when he stepped out to take a call he left the pot on the back burner, carefully, at the lowest flame. When he came back his brother-in-law was standing over it with the salt shaker. "It was a little bland," Kenji said, cheerfully, and put the shaker down. Takeshi tasted it. It tasted like seawater. Every hour of that afternoon, ruined in one flick of the wrist. Takeshi stood perfectly still, his hand gripping the ladle so hard his knuckles cracked. The guests were already in the next room; he could hear his wife laughing. "Did I say you could touch it?" he asked, his voice dangerously soft. Kenji blinked, still smiling. "Just trying to help." Takeshi poured the entire pot into the sink in one long, deliberate motion, steam roaring up around them both, and did not take his eyes off Kenji the whole time.

At six-thirty a text from the guest of honor: oh, by the way, she was vegan now, hope that's okay! Siobhan read it standing in her kitchen surrounded by the beef bourguignon that had been simmering since noon, the butter-laden potato gratin, the cheese plate she'd driven across town for. She'd asked. Two weeks ago she had specifically asked about dietary restrictions, and this exact woman had replied "Nope, I eat anything!" with a little thumbs-up. Siobhan's jaw set. She could feel her pulse beating in her neck. She typed "Of course!" and stared at it, and then deleted it, and put the phone face down on the counter with a sharp crack. Then she yanked open the pantry and began pulling out cans, chickpeas, tomatoes, coconut milk, slamming each one down on the counter like a gavel. Forty minutes. Fine. She would do it in forty minutes, and she would not smile once while doing it.

The apartment in the listing had hardwood floors and a view of the river. The apartment the property manager unlocked for me after I'd driven eleven hours with everything I owned in a rented truck had carpet the color of weak tea, a smell like wet cardboard, and a window that looked directly at a brick wall three feet away. "Same unit number," he said, shrugging. "Different building. The other one got rented." I stood in the doorway holding a lamp, and the lamp started shaking because my hands were. "I signed a lease for that one," I said. "I have the photos. I wired you a deposit for that one." He said there was nothing he could do. My face went hot and my throat clamped shut. I set the lamp down on the floor so I wouldn't swing it, and I took out my phone and started recording him, and I said, "Say that again. Slowly. For the camera."

Moving day in a new city, and the moving company that had loaded Delia's belongings in Atlanta with such warm Southern courtesy now called to say the truck would be "about four days late," and there'd be an additional fee of nine hundred dollars to deliver it at all. Delia was standing in the middle of her empty new living room in Minneapolis with nothing but a sleeping bag and a box of granola bars. She asked them to repeat the number. They repeated it. Her free hand found the windowsill and squeezed until the paint flaked under her nails. "That's not in the contract," she said, and her voice went up an octave. The dispatcher said it was in the fine print, page six. "Read it to me." He did. It wasn't there. "It's not there," she said, and now she was shouting, alone in that echoing room, the sound bouncing back off the bare walls at her.

On my first night in the new place, at two in the morning, the upstairs neighbor started playing the drums. Actual drums. I lay on the mattress on the floor in a city where I knew nobody and listened to the same four bars over and over, the ceiling light fixture trembling with each kick. I'd asked the leasing office about noise. I'd asked twice. They'd said it was a "very quiet building, mostly professionals." At two-twenty I got up and banged on the ceiling with a broom handle. The drumming paused, then came back louder, a little flourish on the cymbal like a reply. My chest went tight, my heartbeat thudding in my ears in time with the bass drum. I yanked on a sweatshirt, marched up the stairwell in bare feet, and hammered on the door with the side of my fist until the drumming stopped and a guy in headphones opened it, looking surprised. I was not surprised. I was done.

Gustavo had carried his grandfather's armchair up five flights of stairs because the elevator, which the landlord swore was "being serviced this week," had a notice taped to it dated last March. Now, sweating through his shirt, he set the chair down in his new living room and noticed that the radiator was gone. Not broken. Gone. Just four bolt holes in the floor and a capped pipe. It was October in Chicago. He called the landlord. "Oh, yeah, we'll get to that," the man said, as if Gustavo had asked about a lightbulb. Gustavo's ears started burning. He'd moved across the country for this job. He'd paid first, last, and security, sight unseen, because the man had been so friendly on video. "When?" Gustavo said. "Give me a date." The landlord laughed and said soon. Gustavo pressed his forehead against the cold window, jaw clenched so hard his ears popped, and repeated, "A date. Today."

I'd chosen this city because my sister lived here. That was the whole point. Leave the job, leave the old apartment, come be near family for once. I spent the morning hauling boxes up the stairs alone, because she'd said she'd come help and then texted that something had "come up." At four I saw her on social media, at a brunch, mimosa in hand, tagged with a group of women laughing. I sat down on a box marked KITCHEN and it caved in under me, and I landed hard on the floor surrounded by broken dishes. I didn't cry. I just sat there, staring at the screen, breathing fast through my teeth, my face burning. I scrolled to the next photo. She was wearing the scarf I'd given her for Christmas. I dialed her and it rang and rang, and when she finally answered, cheerful and a little loud, I said, "How was brunch?" and listened to her go quiet.

The new building's management had given Wanjiru a parking space, number 31, in writing, and every single evening for the first week someone else's silver SUV was in it. She left a polite note. Then a less polite note. On the eighth night she came home from a twelve-hour shift at her new job, in a city where she still got lost every day, and the SUV was there again with her note crumpled under its wiper. She sat behind the wheel with the engine idling and her fingers clamped around the steering wheel, feeling the heat crawl up her neck. A man came down the steps, keys jingling, and walked toward the SUV. She was out of the car before she'd decided to get out. "Is this yours?" He said he didn't see the problem; the spots weren't really assigned. She held up her lease, finger shaking on the line. "It says thirty-one. It says my name. Move it. Now."

Mile twenty-five, and the guy who'd been drafting off me since mile eighteen, tucking right behind my shoulder, letting me break the wind for seven miles, suddenly surged past with a smug little wave. Not a word. Not a thanks. Just that wave, like I was a taxi that had gotten him where he needed to go. Something hot shot up through my chest and into my face. My legs had been screaming for an hour, but now I didn't feel them at all. I gritted my teeth so hard my jaw cramped and I went after him. I didn't care about my time anymore. I cared about his back, the sweaty blue singlet, the number pinned crookedly to it, 4471. I hated that number. I passed him with four hundred meters to go and I didn't wave. I didn't even look. I just heard him wheezing behind me and felt a hard, mean satisfaction burning in my lungs.

Olamide had trained eighteen months for this, and in the last mile a course marshal in a yellow vest stepped out and waved the whole pack of them down a side street, the wrong side street, and it took a quarter mile of confused runners slowing and turning before someone shouted that it was wrong. They had to double back. Olamide's chest heaved. He could see his goal time evaporating on his watch, second by second, three minutes, four. He found the marshal on the way back, standing there sheepishly, and as he passed he screamed at him, actually screamed, a raw sound he didn't recognize, wordless and ragged. Spit flew. His legs were burning, but the burning in his chest was worse. He ran the rest of that mile faster than he'd run any mile all day, fists clenched instead of loose, every stride a stomp, glaring at every orange cone like it had done this to him personally.

In the last mile of the marathon I passed the spot where my ex-husband had promised to stand with our kids and a sign. No kids. No sign. Just an empty piece of curb by the pharmacy, and my phone, when I glanced at it, showing a text from an hour ago: "kids were tired, went home, good luck!!" Good luck. Like I was buying a lottery ticket. I'd told them about this spot for weeks. My daughter had drawn the sign herself. My throat locked and my breath came ragged, and suddenly I was running not with my legs but with something that came up from my stomach, hot and grimly steady. Each footfall slapped the asphalt. I imagined his face on every step. I passed people. I passed a lot of people. I crossed the finish line with my teeth bared, and the volunteer who put the medal around my neck took a step back.

A spectator on a bicycle was weaving through the course in the last mile, filming himself on his phone, and Henrietta had to swerve around him twice, losing her rhythm, her calf threatening to seize. The third time he cut in front of her she clipped his back wheel with her shin and almost went down. She stumbled, caught herself, felt the hot sting of skin torn open on the gear teeth. He didn't even stop. He glanced back and laughed. Henrietta, sixty-three years old and in her first marathon, raised a shaking fist and shouted something she would later be a little ashamed of, loud enough that a whole cluster of spectators cheered. Blood was trickling into her sock. Her breath was sawing in her throat. She kept going, glaring at the back of his helmet as he pedaled away, lips pulled tight over her teeth, and every time she thought about slowing down she saw that laugh again.

The water station at mile twenty-five was empty. Not running low. Empty, the tables bare, a few volunteers standing around chatting with stacks of unfilled cups. Rui had been rationing himself for this station, telling himself he only had to make it to twenty-five, and now his mouth was so dry his tongue stuck to his teeth. "Where's the water?" he croaked. A volunteer shrugged and said they'd run out an hour ago and someone was "bringing more." Rui stared at her. His temples throbbed. "An hour," he rasped. "There are still thousands of us." He grabbed an empty cup off the table and crushed it in his fist and threw it on the ground, and it bounced, pathetically light, which only made it worse. He ran on, mouth parched, legs cramping, cursing under his breath with every step, composing in his head the letter he would send the organizers, line by vicious line.

I'd paid two hundred dollars for this race, and in the last mile the organizers had let the half-marathoners merge onto our route, so suddenly I was weaving through a wall of people walking four abreast, chatting, taking selfies, one guy literally eating a hot dog. I'd been on pace for a qualifying time. I watched it slip away as I dodged, stopped, dodged again. My lungs were burning and my jaw was clamped so tight my teeth ached. "On your left!" I shouted. Nobody moved. "LEFT!" A woman turned and gave me a look like I'd been rude. I squeezed between her and a barrier, scraping my arm on the metal. I didn't feel it. All I felt was this pressure in my chest, swelling with every second I lost, and when I finally crossed the line two minutes over my target I didn't stop for my medal. I went straight to the information tent, still gasping.

Biscuit didn't come when I whistled. I whistled again, louder, and stepped out onto the back porch, and that's when I saw the gate standing wide open. I'd latched it. I always latched it. And then I saw the gardener's truck pulling away from the curb, the same guy I'd told three separate times to close the gate behind him. My heart started pounding, half fear and half something hotter. I ran to the street in my socks, shouting Biscuit's name, and the truck was already at the corner. I chased it. I actually chased it, waving my arms, and when the guy finally stopped and rolled down his window I slapped the side of his door. "The gate," I said, barely able to breathe. "I told you about the gate. My dog is gone." He started to say something and I didn't let him. "Get out and help me look. Right now. You're not leaving until we find her."

Ignatius let the dog out at ten for her last pee, the same as every night, and when he went to call her in five minutes later there was a hole under the back fence that hadn't been there before. A fresh one, dirt still loose. On the other side, the neighbor's yard, where Ignatius had seen the neighbor's teenage son tossing food over the fence all week, despite being asked, twice, to stop. Ignatius's face went hot. He grabbed a flashlight and went out the front door and around the block, every footstep slapping the pavement, and found the boy on the porch, earbuds in, scrolling. "Have you seen my dog?" The boy shrugged without removing an earbud. Ignatius reached over and plucked it out of his ear. "I asked you," he said, low and shaking, "to stop feeding her over the fence. Now she's dug out. She's fourteen. She's half blind. Get your shoes on."

The kids had been told a hundred times: when you let Pepper out, you stand at the door until she comes back. A hundred times. And at five o'clock, when Laila called the dog for dinner and got nothing but silence, she found both children on the couch with a tablet, and the back door wide open, and the yard empty. "Who let her out?" Silence. "Who let her out?" Her voice cracked off the walls and both children flinched. Her heart was racing, her hands cold, her face hot. She didn't wait for an answer. She grabbed the leash off the hook so hard the hook came out of the wall. The plaster crumbled and dusted the floor. "Shoes on," she said, through her teeth. "Both of you. Now. You're going to walk every street with me until we find her, and if it gets dark, you'll walk them in the dark." Neither child argued.

My dog was in my neighbor's garage. I found that out after forty-five minutes of searching, calling, crying, knocking on doors, after I'd printed flyers and called the shelter. I found it out because I heard her barking, muffled, and followed the sound, and when I pounded on Ruth Ann's side door she opened it and said, "Oh! Is she yours? She was wandering, so I kept her safe." Wandering. In a yard with a six-foot fence. Ruth Ann had complained about the barking every week for a year. I felt a hot, prickling flush climb up my whole body. "You saw me," I said. "You saw me walk past your house four times calling her name." She fluttered her hands. I pushed past her into the garage and there was Juniper, tied to a pipe with a piece of rope, tail going crazy. My hands were shaking so hard I couldn't untie the knot. I had to cut it with my car key.

It was the electric company. Ondine figured that out within ten minutes of noticing her dog hadn't come back in: a technician had come to read the meter, propped the side gate open, and left it that way. She found the work order flapping on her door. Kasper was a skittish rescue, terrified of traffic, and the road at the end of the lane was a highway. Her throat went tight. She called the utility, and while the hold music played she was already striding down the lane in her slippers, calling Kasper's name until her voice went raw. When a customer service rep finally answered and asked for her account number, Ondine stopped in the middle of the gravel and shouted into the phone so loudly that a crow lifted off the fence beside her. "Your man left my gate open and my dog is gone. I don't want an account number. I want him back here looking."

Teodor had told his roommate, in plain words, that the latch on the yard gate was broken and that the dog couldn't be left out unsupervised until he fixed it on Saturday. So when he came home on Thursday and found Moose's water bowl full and untouched and the yard silent, and the roommate on the couch with his headphones on, Teodor felt a slow, hot pressure build from his stomach up into his chest. He pulled the headphones off. "Where's Moose?" The roommate blinked. "Out back? I let him out like an hour ago." "An hour." Teodor's hands were trembling. "I told you the gate was broken. I wrote it on a sign. I taped the sign to the door." He held up the sign, which had fallen to the floor and been stepped on, a muddy footprint across the words DO NOT. He crushed it in his fist. "Get up," he said, his voice cracking. "Get up and find my dog."

Ten minutes before my set, the sound guy told me my monitor wouldn't work tonight. I asked why. He said the headliner's band had "borrowed" it. I looked across the stage and there it was, my wedge monitor, sitting in front of their drummer's kit, a strip of their gaffer tape across the top. I'd been promised that monitor in writing. I'd driven three hours for this slot. Without it I'd be singing blind, unable to hear my own pitch over the house mix. My face went hot and my fingers tightened on the neck of my guitar until the strings bit grooves into my fingertips. I walked over to the drummer, who was eating chips, and I said, "That's mine." He said they needed it. "So did I," I said. "That's why I asked for it two weeks ago." I picked it up myself and carried it back across the stage, cables dragging, and I didn't apologize for the noise.

Five minutes before curtain, Aleksandra opened her violin case and found the bridge snapped clean in half, the strings slack and tangled. The case had been in the green room. Only the orchestra had been in the green room. Only one person in the orchestra had wanted her solo: Petra, who was now tuning across the room, very carefully not looking over. Aleksandra's chest went tight and hot, her breath shallow. She lifted the broken pieces, turned them in the light. A clean break. Not a fall. Her hands began to shake, not with nerves now but with something sharper, something that made her want to walk across the room and hold the pieces up to Petra's face. She didn't. Instead she called the stage manager over, her voice low and hard, and asked for the backup instrument, and while she waited she stared straight at Petra until Petra's bow skittered off the string in a squeal.

The promoter came backstage while I was warming up and said, by the way, they'd cut my set from forty minutes to fifteen because the headliner wanted more time. Fifteen. I'd sold forty tickets myself, hustled every friend and coworker and cousin. I'd built a whole arc into that set, the quiet songs, the build, the new piece I'd written for my father. "You can't do fifteen minutes of a forty-minute show," I said. He said that was the situation. I could feel my heart punching against my ribs. My hands, which had been cold with nerves a minute ago, were hot and tingling now. "Then give me back the ticket money," I said. He laughed. He actually laughed and patted my shoulder and walked off. I stood there with my jaw clenched so tight it clicked, breathing hard through my nose, the setlist crumpling in my fist. Then I smoothed it out on my knee and crossed off everything but the loudest songs.

Bongani was halfway through tuning his bass when the club owner wandered in and mentioned, casually, that the band would be paid in drink tickets tonight instead of the two hundred dollars they'd agreed on. "Cash flow thing," he said. "You understand." Bongani's fingers stilled on the tuning peg. He thought of the van rental, the gas, the drummer who'd taken an unpaid day off work to be here. The heat came up through his chest so fast he had to set the bass down against the amp. "We had a deal," he said. "We shook on it." The owner shrugged, smiling. "Shook on it" meant nothing to him; Bongani could see that in his face. Bongani stood up to his full height, which was considerable, and the owner's smile thinned. "Then we don't play," Bongani said, his voice rumbling low. "Tell your crowd. You go out there and tell them why." The owner's eyes darted to the packed room.

Fifteen minutes before the recital, my piano teacher leaned into the practice room and told me she'd switched the program order, so I'd now be playing right after Clementine Ashworth, the conservatory's prize student, instead of at the start like we'd planned for months. "It'll be good for you," she said. "A challenge." I sat at the piano bench with my hands frozen over the keys and felt my face burn. She knew. She knew how I'd struggled with nerves all year, how carefully we'd placed me first so I wouldn't have to sit and listen and compare. She'd done it on purpose. I could tell from the little smile. I pressed down on the keys without playing, a silent chord, harder and harder until my wrists ached. When she left, I stood and kicked the bench back so it scraped across the floor, then sat again. Fine. I'd play after Clementine. And I'd play it loud.

Just before Itzel stepped onstage, her bandmate Rory leaned over and whispered that he'd invited her ex to the show. "Thought it'd be fun," he said, grinning. "Closure, you know?" Itzel looked past the curtain and there he was, front row, arms folded, the man who'd told her for three years that her songs were "cute." Something cold and then very hot flooded through her body, starting in her stomach and burning out to her fingertips. She turned to Rory. "You did what?" Her voice came out so sharp the stage manager looked up from her clipboard. Rory's grin faded. "I didn't think—" "No," Itzel said, "you didn't." She gripped the mic stand so hard its clamp creaked. Her pulse was roaring. When the lights came up she walked out to center stage, looked straight down at the front row, and played the first chord so hard a string snapped.

The box on my doorstep was addressed to me, but I hadn't ordered anything, and when I opened it I found a brand-new phone, top of the line, and a receipt charged to my credit card. Eleven hundred dollars. Shipped to me, ordered from my account, at three in the morning. I stood on the porch with the packing peanuts blowing around my ankles and felt my stomach drop and then flood with heat. My nephew had stayed over that night. My nephew, who'd asked to "borrow my laptop to check something." I called my sister. She said I must be mistaken. "He's sixteen," she said, "he wouldn't." I read her the order confirmation, the time stamp, the shipping note: "Leave at door, do not ring." My voice was shaking now, getting louder with every word. "He set it to come here so he could pick it up before I noticed," I said. "He planned it." The phone in my hand felt like evidence.

Ottilie didn't recognize the return address, so she opened the package at the kitchen counter with a butter knife and found, nestled in tissue paper, her own grandmother's silver locket. The one her cousin Beatrice had sworn, at the funeral, she had never seen. There was a note in Beatrice's looping hand: "Found this in my things, thought you might want it! Hugs." Found it. Ottilie lifted the locket by its chain and watched it turn in the light. Four years.
