Four years of Beatrice shaking her head sadly every Christmas when the subject came up, wondering aloud where it could have gone. Ottilie's fingers tightened around the chain until it pressed red lines into her palm. Her heart was pounding. She picked up her phone and typed "Hugs" back, just that, and then deleted it, and then typed a much longer message, every sentence jabbing, and sent it before she could change her mind.

The package was from my ex-wife: a cardboard box full of everything I'd left behind in the divorce, the stuff she'd sworn she'd already thrown out. My records. My father's watch. The letters my son wrote me from camp. All of it, eighteen months later, with no note, and when I lifted out the records I saw that she'd stacked them on their sides with something heavy on top. Every single one was warped. I held up my father's copy of Kind of Blue, rippled like a potato chip, and something hot and hard rose up the back of my throat. I set it down. I picked up the next one. Ruined. And the next. My hands were trembling by the fifth, and by the tenth I'd stopped looking and was just breathing, loud and fast through my nose, my fist pressed against the cardboard flap until it tore. She'd wanted me to know. That was the point of the box.

Two days after Nikolai told his downstairs neighbor, for the third time, that the man's music was too loud, a package appeared outside his door: a pair of cheap foam earplugs and a printed card that read "For the sensitive one :)". No name, but there didn't need to be one. Nikolai stood in the hallway staring at it, and his face went hot, prickling all the way to his ears. He'd been polite. He'd brought cookies the first time. He picked up the earplugs and crushed them in his fist until they compressed into nothing, then let go and watched them slowly swell back. That made it worse somehow. He walked down the stairs, each step loud on purpose, and knocked on the door below with the flat of his hand. When the man opened it, grinning, Nikolai held the card up an inch from his nose. "Funny," he said, in a voice that made the grin falter. "Very funny. Let's talk."

Inés hadn't ordered anything, so when the courier handed her a parcel from her mother-in-law she opened it on the doorstep, puzzled. Inside: a book titled How to Keep Your Husband Happy, gift-wrapped, with a sticky note on the cover. "Thought this might help, dear!" Inés stood very still on the front step with the wind tugging at the wrapping paper. Her cheeks were burning. Her mother-in-law had been at their house last Sunday, watching her cook, commenting on the salt, on the curtains, on the fact that Inés worked full time. And now this. Inés felt her fingers digging into the book's cover, bending the cardboard. She marched into the house and dropped it on the table in front of her husband, so hard his coffee jumped. "Your mother," she said, and couldn't finish, because her throat had gone tight and her voice wouldn't hold. She jabbed a finger at the note. He read it, and she watched him, waiting.

The box was sitting on my porch with the lid already cut open. Not torn, cut, a neat line with a blade, and when I lifted the flaps there was nothing inside but crumpled paper and the packing slip for the camera lens I'd saved four months to buy. The tracking said delivered at 2:14. The neighbor's doorbell camera, pointing right at my door, would have seen everything. I knocked on his door, holding the empty box, and he said, without even looking at it, that his camera "wasn't working that day." I stood there with my heart thudding and my face going hot and I said, "It was working when it caught my cat last week. You sent me the video." He shrugged. I could feel my teeth grinding. "Check it," I said. "Check it right now, or I call the police and they check it." He started to close the door. I put my foot in it.

My brother had already been through the house before I got there. I could tell because the jewelry box on Nana's dresser was empty, and the good china was gone from the cabinet, and there were clean rectangles on the wallpaper where her paintings used to hang. Victor came in from the garage carrying a box of her paperbacks, cheerful as anything. "Figured I'd get a head start," he said. I stood in the doorway of her bedroom and felt my hands start to shake. "Where are the rings?" He said he'd put them "somewhere safe." I said safe where, and he got vague, and the vaguer he got the hotter my face got until I was shouting, actually shouting, in my dead grandmother's bedroom. "She said the garnet was mine. She said it in front of you. At Easter. You were sitting right there." He set the box down and wouldn't look at me, and that told me everything.

The three of them had agreed: nothing gets taken until everyone's in the room. So when Seo-yeon arrived at their grandmother's apartment and found her younger sister wrapping the jade figurines in newspaper and packing them into her own car, she stopped dead in the hallway. "We agreed," Seo-yeon said. Min-ji didn't even pause. "You don't even like them." Seo-yeon felt her face burn, a hot pressure rising behind her eyes. It wasn't about liking them. It was about Halmeoni's hands taking them down every New Year's to dust them while she told stories about each one. Seo-yeon crossed the room in three long strides and took the next figurine right out of her sister's hands. "Put them back," she said, her voice so low and tight it barely carried. "All of them. Unwrap them and put them back exactly where she had them." Min-ji laughed. Seo-yeon didn't. She held out her hand and waited.

We'd been at it for six hours, me and my two brothers, in Grandma Edie's tiny house that still smelled like lavender and burnt toast, and every single time I picked something up, Lionel said, "Oh, I was going to take that." Her sewing box. Her cookbook. Her reading glasses, for God's sake. He didn't sew. He didn't cook. He'd visited her twice in five years. I was the one who drove her to every appointment, every Thursday, the last three years of her life. When I reached for her quilt and he said it again, "I was going to take that," something inside me finally gave way. I threw the quilt down on the bed. "You were going to take everything," I said, too loud, and my voice was shaking. "You didn't come when she was alive and now you want her reading glasses?" Lionel opened his mouth. I pointed at the door, hand trembling. "Out. Go sit in your car."

Reuben found the will on the third day, folded inside their grandmother's Bible, dated two months before she died, and it was different from the one their cousin had filed with the court. Very different. In this one, the cottage by the lake went to all four grandchildren equally. In the one the cousin filed, it went entirely to the cousin. Reuben read it twice standing in the dim spare room, and then he went downstairs to his sister, who was sorting dishes, and laid it on the table between them without a word. Imogen read it. He watched her shoulders go rigid and her face flush dark red. "She knew about this," Imogen said, her voice very quiet and very hard. "Sabine sat with Gran every day that last month. She knew." Reuben nodded. His own jaw ached from clenching. Imogen set down the plate she'd been holding, carefully, and then picked up her phone.

"You're keeping the piano," my sister said, not a question, and I said yes, because Abuela had told me herself, many times, that the piano was mine, that I was the only one who'd ever practiced. And then Valentina said, very calmly, that she'd already sold it. Sold it. To a dealer. Last week. The truck was coming Saturday. I stood in Abuela's living room next to that piano, my hand resting on its lid, and felt the blood drain out of my face and then rush back in so hot I could barely see. "You sold it," I said. "Before the funeral flowers were even dead." She said we needed the money for the estate costs. "We? You didn't ask me. You didn't ask anyone." I could hear my own voice rising, cracking, echoing in that half-empty room. I slammed the piano lid shut, and the strings inside hummed for a long time, a low, discordant chord that wouldn't stop.

Felix was boxing up their grandmother's kitchen when his older brother came in with a stack of colored sticky notes and began labeling furniture: a green note for himself on the dining table, a green note on the grandfather clock, a green note on the rocking chair. "Green's mine," Laurent said breezily. "Pick a color." Felix put down the roll of packing tape very slowly. His stomach was knotting up, heat spreading up his neck. Laurent had missed the funeral. He'd sent flowers and a text. Felix had been the one holding her hand in the hospice. "You weren't here," Felix said. Laurent waved that away. "Work, you know how it is." Felix walked over to the rocking chair and peeled the green note off and crumpled it into a ball. Then the clock. Then the table. He threw the little green wad at his brother's chest, and it bounced off and fell to the floor between them.

I unlocked the front door of the bakery at five-thirty on Monday and stepped straight into an inch of water. The walk-in freezer door was standing open. Everything inside, the butter, the doughs, the cream, two thousand dollars of product, was soft and dripping and warm. My weekend closer, Brayden, had texted on Saturday night: "all locked up boss!" with a thumbs up. I stood there in the dark with water soaking into my sneakers and felt my whole chest clench, my breath coming hot and short. I flipped on the lights so hard the switch plate cracked. Then I sloshed over to the freezer and looked inside and saw his phone charger plugged into the outlet by the door, which meant he'd propped it open to charge his phone. I picked up the charger and yanked it out of the wall and squeezed it in my fist until the plastic edges dug into my palm. Then I called him. He didn't answer. I kept calling.

Ngozi arrived at her boutique at eight on Monday to find that the new coffee chain next door had, over the weekend, installed its outdoor seating directly in front of her display window. Six tables. Twelve chairs. A large chalkboard sign advertising pumpkin lattes, positioned precisely where it blocked her mannequins. Ngozi stood on the sidewalk with her keys in her hand and her bag sliding off her shoulder and felt heat surge up from her collar. She'd been on this block eleven years. She walked into the coffee shop, past the line, straight to the counter. "Who's the manager?" A young man raised his hand uncertainly. "Your tables are on my frontage," she said, and her voice was clipped and very loud. "You'll move them, and you'll move them before I open at nine." He said corporate had approved the layout. She leaned across the counter. "Then call corporate. I'll wait." She didn't move.

Monday morning at the hardware store, and the first thing Clyde saw when he rolled up the security grate was the graffiti: a huge, sprawling tag across his front window, sprayed right over the gold lettering his father had painted by hand in 1971. Clyde dropped the grate handle. It clattered back down halfway. He stood there with his coffee cooling in his hand, breathing heavily, staring at the dripping purple paint, and felt the cup crumple in his grip. Hot coffee ran over his fingers. He didn't notice. That lettering had survived two floods and a recession. He'd touched it up himself every spring with a brush the size of a pencil. He set what was left of the cup down on the sidewalk, very carefully, and pulled out his phone and started taking pictures, one after another, jaw clenched so hard a muscle jumped in his cheek. He knew the tag. He'd seen it on the bus shelter across the street.

The landlord had changed the locks. That's how my Monday started: me, at my own bookshop's door at nine a.m., with a key that didn't fit, and a notice taped to the glass saying I was in breach of lease for "late payment." I wasn't late. I'd paid on the first, same as always, by bank transfer, and I had the confirmation on my phone. I pulled it up and pressed it against the glass, as if the empty shop could read it. My hands were trembling. Through the window I could see my cat, Tolstoy, sitting on the counter, staring out at me, waiting for breakfast. That was what did it. My vision went hot and blurry. I called the landlord and when he answered I didn't say hello. "My cat is locked inside," I said. "You have one hour to open this door, and then I break the glass and send you the bill." I meant every word of it.

Oyelaran opened the shop at seven, same as every Monday, and found that the inventory app showed forty units of the new headphones sold over the weekend. Forty. The register showed nine. He went to the back room and counted the shelf twice, his lips moving, his heart beating harder with each empty slot. Thirty-one gone. Only two people had weekend keys: himself and his nephew Sola, whom he'd hired as a favor to his sister. Oyelaran sat down on an overturned crate. He felt the heat rise from his stomach into his face, a slow tide. He thought about the speech he'd given Sola on his first day, about trust, about family, and how the boy had nodded so earnestly. He pulled up the security footage on his phone, scrolled to Saturday night, and watched his nephew carry box after box out the back door. His thumb pressed the screen so hard the image froze.

I pulled into the strip mall at seven on Monday and found the delivery I'd been waiting three weeks for sitting outside my flower shop, on the sidewalk, in the rain, where it had apparently been since Friday afternoon. Six boxes of imported tulips. The cardboard was soaked through, sagging, and when I lifted a flap the stems were black and slimy. The driver hadn't called. He hadn't knocked on the dry cleaner's next door, who'd signed for me a hundred times. He'd just dumped them. I stood there in the drizzle with my umbrella drooping and felt something clench hard in my gut. Valentine's Day was Wednesday. I had preorders for two hundred bouquets. I kicked the nearest box, not hard, but it split open anyway and spilled ruined flowers across the wet pavement, and I stood there staring at them, my breath fogging in short, ragged bursts, before I dialed the distributor with numb, shaking fingers.

I'd been volunteering at the food bank every Saturday for two years, and that morning I watched a man in a pressed golf shirt pull up in a new SUV, load his trunk with three boxes of donated groceries meant for families, and drive off waving. The coordinator saw it too, and shrugged. "We don't check," she said. I stood at the folding table with a can of green beans in each hand and felt my face burn. Behind me in line was a woman with two toddlers who'd waited forty minutes in the cold, and when she got to the front we were out of the protein boxes. Out. Because that guy had taken three. I set the cans down hard, one, two, and they rolled. "We should check," I said, and my voice came out much louder than I meant, and the coordinator looked startled. "We absolutely should check." I gave the woman my own lunch from my bag.

Thomasina had organized the whole Thanksgiving drive herself, called every grocery store in the county, wheedled donations out of every church, and on the morning of the giveaway a city councilman showed up with a photographer. He put on an apron over his suit, posed handing a turkey to a smiling child, shook a few hands, and was gone in eight minutes. That evening the local news ran the photo under the headline "Councilman Feeds Hundreds." Thomasina watched it on the TV in the food bank's back office and felt her shoulders creep up toward her ears. Her jaw locked. Her name wasn't anywhere. Neither were the names of the forty volunteers who'd stood in the cold since dawn. She switched off the television with a jab so hard the remote skittered across the desk. Then she sat down at the computer and began typing a letter to the editor, her fingers hammering the keys, the first sentence already blunt enough to blister.

A woman came through the line at the food bank and the volunteer beside me, an older man named Hollis, looked at her nice coat and said, loud enough for the whole line to hear, "Some people don't look that hungry to me." The woman's face crumpled. She put back the bag she'd just taken. I watched her walk away, shoulders hunched, and something went white-hot inside my chest. I didn't think. I put down the clipboard and turned on him. "That coat might be the only warm thing she owns," I said. "You don't know anything about her." He started to say something about freeloaders, and I stepped right up to him, close enough to see the broken veins in his nose. "Not here," I said. My voice was shaking. "Not while you're wearing that apron." Then I went out into the parking lot after her, half running, and caught her by the bus stop, and handed her the bag.

Arjun had spent all Saturday morning sorting donated cans, and at noon he came across an entire box of them that had expired in 2014. Dented, bulging, rusted. Under the cans was a receipt from a local company, the kind that gets a tax deduction for donating, with a handwritten note: "clearing the warehouse, ha." Ha. He stared at it for a long moment, his pulse thumping in his neck. Families would have eaten this. Kids. He picked up a bulging can of soup and turned it over in his hand, and his grip tightened until the swollen metal creaked. He took the whole box, all forty pounds of it, and carried it out to the dumpster, and then he stood there and decided against the dumpster. He carried it to his car instead. He knew where that company's office was. He was going to set the box on their front desk on Monday morning, right in front of whoever answered.

The new volunteer supervisor at the food bank had decided that clients would have to show photo ID and proof of address before they could take anything home. Starting today. No warning. Esperanza stood at her station and watched the line stall, watched an elderly man pat his pockets, confused, watched a teenage girl with a baby on her hip go red and turn around and leave. Esperanza's fists clenched at her sides. Her neck was hot under her collar. She marched to the supervisor's table. "Half these people don't have an address," she said. "That's why they're here." He said it was about preventing fraud. "Fraud," she repeated, and her voice cracked like a whip, and the whole line went quiet. "That girl with the baby is fraud? Mr. Pak, who's been coming for six years, is fraud?" He shuffled his papers. She picked up a stack of ID forms off his table and dropped them in the recycling bin.

I volunteered at the food bank on my day off, three hours sorting produce, and at the end of the shift I found out the manager had been taking the best of the donations home every Friday. Not stealing, exactly. He called it "perishables management." The fresh berries, the good cheese, the pastries from the French bakery downtown. Everything that families waited in line for and never saw. I found the cooler in his truck because he'd asked me to help him load it. I stood there in the parking lot holding a crate of strawberries and felt something hot and hard spread through my ribs. "These were for the Hernandez kids," I said. "She asked me about strawberries last week. I told her we never get any." He laughed and said I should take some too. I put the crate down on the asphalt, very carefully, and stepped back, and stared at him until he stopped laughing.

We'd been in the emergency waiting room for six hours, my son's arm swollen and purple in a sling made from my scarf, when a man in a suit walked in, spoke quietly to the receptionist, and was taken back within five minutes. Five. I watched the doors swing shut behind him and felt my jaw lock so hard my ears popped. My son was eleven. He'd stopped crying around hour three and was now just pale and silent, which was worse. I walked up to the desk. "Who was that?" The receptionist said she couldn't discuss other patients. "Was his arm broken?" She said she couldn't discuss other patients. My hands were flat on the counter and they were trembling. "My son has a bone pushing against his skin," I said, and my voice was rising, and I didn't care who heard. "I want a doctor out here. Now. Not in an hour. Now."

Leopold had been in the surgical waiting room for four hours when the nurse finally came out and told him his wife's operation had been "pushed back." Not finished. Not even started. Pushed back, because a different surgeon had run over. Four hours he'd been sitting in that molded plastic chair, his wife's handbag in his lap, drinking vending-machine coffee and watching the door. "Nobody told me," he said. The nurse said she was telling him now. Leopold felt the blood come into his face, his hands closing around the handbag strap until it creaked. "She hasn't eaten since last night," he said. "She's lying back there frightened and starving, and nobody told either of us anything." His voice was climbing. A child across the room stopped playing with her toy and stared at him. "I want to see her. Right now. I want to sit with her while she waits." The nurse began to say that wasn't possible, and he stood up.

The family in the waiting room next to me had been on speakerphone for an hour. Loud speakerphone, an argument about a car loan, while I sat there with my hands folded waiting for news about my father's heart. Twice I'd asked them, nicely, to take it outside. Twice the woman had rolled her eyes and kept going. When she laughed, a big careless honk of a laugh, right as a doctor came out and called someone else's name, I felt something snap inside my chest. My pulse was pounding in my temples. I stood up and crossed the room in three steps and stood in front of her. "My father," I said, "is having open-heart surgery behind that door. Some of us in this room are waiting to find out if people we love are alive. Hang up the phone." My voice cracked on the last word and came out much louder than I meant. The room went silent. She hung up.

Rania had asked the front desk four times for an update on her mother. Each time, the clerk smiled the same professional smile and told her someone would be out "shortly." Shortly had now lasted three hours and twenty minutes. Rania's leg was bouncing so hard the row of linked chairs rattled. Then she saw it: her mother's name on the whiteboard behind the desk, with "discharged" written next to it in blue marker. Discharged. Her mother had been released over an hour ago, alone, confused, seventy-eight years old and without her glasses, and no one had come out to the waiting room to tell her daughter. Rania stood up so fast her purse spilled onto the floor. She didn't pick it up. "Where is she?" she demanded, her voice ringing off the tile. The clerk's smile faltered. "You discharged her. Where did she go? Who did she leave with?" Rania's hands were shaking as she gripped the counter.

The vending machine ate my last two dollars. I'd been in that waiting room since midnight, my wife somewhere behind the double doors with a fever of a hundred and four, and the only thing I'd wanted in five hours was a bottle of water, and the machine took my money and gave me nothing. I pressed the button again. Nothing. I pressed the coin return. Nothing. Something hot crawled up the back of my neck. I hit the side of the machine with the flat of my hand, hard, and it rattled, and the bottle stayed exactly where it was, dangling from its coil, mocking me. I hit it again. And again, harder, both hands, until a security guard appeared beside me with his palm out. "Sir." I turned and stared at him, breathing hard, my hands still braced against the glass. "Five hours," I said. "Five hours, and nobody's told me anything." My voice broke.

Sunniva watched the receptionist call the next name, and it wasn't her brother's, again, and she felt her teeth grind together until her jaw ached. They had come in at seven. It was now past eleven. Halvard was slumped against her shoulder, gray-faced, sweating, clutching his stomach, and twice now she'd seen people who'd arrived after them, people with coughs, people chatting on their phones, called through those doors first. She'd asked at the desk. She'd been told triage was based on severity. Well. She looked at her brother, who'd stopped answering questions an hour ago. She stood up so abruptly that her chair screeched across the floor and went to the desk and put both palms down on it, hard. "He's getting worse," she said. "Look at him. Actually look." The receptionist began to recite the triage policy, and Sunniva's voice cut across her, sharp and loud. "No. Stop reading. Look at him."
